_meta.warning: Every figure below is a published estimate, not a quoted price. No microreactor has sold power commercially, so no realised LCOE exists anywhere in this table. Ranges are wide because they encode different assumptions about FOAK vs Nth-of-a-kind cost maturity — that spread IS the finding, not noise to average away.
_meta.review: Reviewed 2026-08-21 against an energy/project-finance reading (three corrections: overstated diesel comparison, false capex sensitivity, missing PTC scope). Citation audit, same day: two capex-scenario rows were removed entirely — their $5,000/kW and $2,500/kW inputs and $80–90 / $35 per MWh outputs appear nowhere in the paper they cited (its capital-cost distribution is $2,500–4,000/kW, treated as nth-of-a-kind). They are replaced by the NEI 2019 FOAK/NOAK bands, which are real published figures. The Alaska row was re-sourced for the same reason: the cited paper never mentions Alaska; the band now comes from sources that do.

microreactor_lcoe.basis: NEI reference plant: two co-located 5 MWe reactors, 40-year life, 10-year core, 95% capacity factor, built on proprietary developer cost data

source.label: NEI — Cost Competitiveness of Micro-Reactors for Remote Markets (2019)

microreactor_lcoe.caveat: This is where the FOAK numbers on this page come from: an NEI study built on proprietary cost data from several microreactor developers. It is the root source most later papers (including the U-Michigan optimization below) cite for capital cost.

microreactor_lcoe.basis: Same NEI reference plant with a 15% learning rate applied FOAK→NOAK, easing to 5–15% after the first 50 units

source.label: NEI — Cost Competitiveness of Micro-Reactors for Remote Markets (2019)

microreactor_lcoe.basis: Market-review estimate; comparable to or below diesel-based electricity in remote locations

source.label: Nuclear Business Platform — microreactor market review

microreactor_lcoe.basis: Genetic-algorithm optimization over design parameters; capital cost drawn from a $2,500–4,000/kW (nominal $3,000) nth-of-a-kind distribution, itself sourced to the NEI study above. The paper reports the PTC cutting LCOE by 22–24%, so the same optimization unsubsidised lands near $63–103/MWh (derived, not published).

source.label: Abdussami et al., Nuclear Engineering and Design (arXiv 2506.13361)

microreactor_lcoe.caveat: The PTC is a U.S. federal incentive and does not apply to the international track. Any export case should be read against the unsubsidised bands. See the incentives note below for why the PTC is still alive for nuclear after the 2025 budget law.

incentives.question: Is the PTC still relevant in 2026, after the One Big Beautiful Bill Act?
incentives.answer: Yes, for nuclear specifically. The OBBBA (signed July 2025) terminated the tech-neutral §45Y/§48E credits early for wind and solar but kept them for nuclear: a nuclear plant qualifies if construction begins before 2034, with a three-year phase-out after that. The deployments this site tracks target operation between 2028 and 2030, comfortably inside that window; most rows publish no construction date, so start-of-construction timing is an open item per project.

points.fact: §45Y/§48E survive for new nuclear that begins construction before 2034, then phase out over three years; the emissions-based sunset trigger was replaced by these fixed dates.

source.label: Morgan Lewis — OBBBA impact on nuclear tax incentives (July 2025)

points.fact: New 10% credit adder for facilities in “nuclear energy communities” (metro areas with ≥0.17% direct nuclear employment since 2010), §45Y only.

source.label: Morgan Lewis — OBBBA impact on nuclear tax incentives

points.fact: New risk: foreign-entity-of-concern (FEOC) restrictions apply from 2026: material-assistance thresholds on the supply chain that a HALEU/TRISO vendor has to clear to keep the credit.

source.label: Morgan Lewis — OBBBA impact on nuclear tax incentives

points.fact: Credit transferability (§6418) survives, except transfers to specified foreign entities; advanced nuclear companies also gain master-limited-partnership eligibility from 2026.

source.label: Morgan Lewis — OBBBA impact on nuclear tax incentives

incentives.caveat: A DoD contractor-owned/contractor-operated unit still needs tax capacity or a transfer counterparty to monetise the credit.

displaced_alternatives.note: These grids run on diesel. NEI puts remote-arctic diesel generation at $0.30–0.60/kWh; Alaska's own Power Cost Equalization reporting shows rural rates of $0.55–0.80+/kWh, with some villages above $1/kWh. The PCE subsidy (FY2026 base 20.38¢/kWh) covers only residential use up to 750 kWh/month. Commercial and industrial loads pay the full unsubsidised rate, which is the price a microreactor has to beat.

reading: Where the bands overlap is what matters. Against **rural Alaska** ($300–800+/MWh, diesel-fired, and commercial loads get no PCE subsidy) even the **FOAK band** ($140–410) wins across most of the range. That is the one uncontested market, and it is why Fort Wainwright is the most interesting row in the Army Janus table. Against **remote diesel** generally ($250–400) the FOAK band overlaps: a first unit at the top of its range ($410) loses to diesel at the bottom of its range ($250), so 'cheaper than diesel' is a site-by-site claim that turns on local fuel logistics until NOAK costs ($90–330) arrive. Against grid-connected U.S. industrial power the microreactor loses in every published case except the PTC-supported optimization ($48–78), which is forward-looking and U.S.-only. So the commercial logic flips by sector: off-grid sites can buy on cost today, while on-grid sites buy on resilience, speed-to-power or carbon and pay a premium for it.
